text: Πρὸς Πέτρον Ἰλλούστριον. Nomen dignitatis est. Basil. Eccl. 7 : Οἱ ἀπὸ πατρικίων ἕως ἰλλουστρίων εἰσὶν οἱ συγκλητικοί. Justin. Novella 13 : Ἡμεῖς γὰρ οὐδενὶ τὴν εἰρημένην ἀρχὴν παραδώσομεν πλὴν εἰ μὴ τῶν μεγαλοπρεπεστάτων ἰλλουστρίων. Erat igitur Petrus hic τῶν ἐν ἀρχῇ, homo senatorii ordinis; nempe εὐγενής, ut Glossæ Basilic. Vir nobilis, et quod præcipuum, spectatæ fidei et probæ orthodoxus, cujus alia nescimus, quam quæ Maximus una et altera epist. de illo insinuavit.
anchorLine: Τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς Πέτρον Ἰλλούστριον (a)
en: To Peter Illustrius. The name of a dignity. Basil. Eccl. 7: those from the patricians up to the illustrii are the senators. Justinian, Novella 13: for we shall hand over the said office to no one except one of the most magnificent illustrii. So this Peter was one of those in office, a man of senatorial rank, that is well-born, as the Basilic Gloss has it. A nobleman and, above all, of approved faith and sound orthodoxy; we know nothing else of him than what Maximus has hinted in one or two letters.

text: Κατὰ ποῖον καὶ ποῖον λόγον. Apta satis repetitio, etsi eam cod. Venet. non habet, sed solum κατὰ ποῖον λόγον. Quod tamen toto discursu Maximus καὶ τρόπον adjunxerit, verisimile est hic scripsisse, κατὰ ποῖον τρόπον καὶ ποῖον λόγον, exque repetita voce, proclivi errore, alterum excidisse.
anchorLine: σκοπῆσαι, κατὰ ποῖον καὶ ποῖον λόγον (v) ἓν ἐστιν
en: 'In what respect and in what respect.' The repetition is apt enough, even though the Venice codex lacks it and has only 'in what respect' (κατὰ ποῖον λόγον). But since Maximus adds 'and manner' (καὶ τρόπον) throughout the discussion, it is likely that he wrote here 'in what manner and in what respect', and that through the repeated word the other term dropped out by an easy error.

text: Τὸν μυθευόμενον ὄρνιθα τὸν Φοίνικα. Laudanda maxime Maximi ἀκρίβεια, qui Patrum fere unus phœnicis avis fabulam aperte exploserit, cum reliqui vel admiscerint, vel certe in dubio rem reliquerint, communique famæ permiscerint. Præcipuus est Clemens Rom. qui ævi simplicitate in sua ad Corinthios epistola, quod unum ejus genuinum monumentum ad nos pervenit, ὡς πανἀληθεστάτῳ, τῷ κατὰ τὸν φοίνικα τὸν ὄρνεον ὑποδείγματι κέχρηται: quod phœnicem avem adhibet, ut verissimum exemplum, inquit Phot., hoc ei nomine dicam scribens. Tertulliano et Epiphanio imposuit locus Scripturæ male intellectus; Cyrillo, Clemens : Maximus rei absurditatem quasi φυσικώτερον explosit, tantamque advertit, ut impugnando vereatur, ne quasi demens prudentibus risum moveat; qui scilicet sic inutili argumento otium terat. Commento occasionem fecit ὁμωνυμία vocis φοῖνιξ, qua sæpe usi οἱ LXX non ut avem significarent, sed ut palmam, quæ ipsa quasi ex se sic renascatur et pullulet. Multis prosecutus hoc argumentum Bocharlus tom. altero de animalibus sacræ Scripturæ, quo ipso laudat Andreæ Schottani Eptaemeram, diatr. 13.
anchorLine: ὄρνιθα τὸν φοίνικα (x), καθάπερ τι μέγα καὶ ἄμα-
en: 'The fabled bird, the phoenix.' Maximus's precision is especially to be praised: almost alone of the Fathers he openly rejects the fable of the phoenix, whereas the rest either mixed it in or at least left the matter in doubt and blended it with common report. Chief among them is Clement of Rome who, in his simplicity of age, in his Epistle to the Corinthians (the only genuine work of his to reach us) uses the example of the phoenix bird as most true; and Photius says that, in writing so, he uses this as an example. The passage of Scripture misunderstood misled Tertullian and Epiphanius; Clement misled Cyril. Maximus rejects the absurdity as rather natural-historical, and takes care in attacking it not to seem a madman to the prudent, who would waste time on a pointless argument. The occasion was the homonymy of the word φοῖνιξ, which the Seventy often used not for the bird but for the palm, which as it were renews itself and sprouts again. Bochart treated this argument at length in vol. 2 of his work on the animals of sacred Scripture, praising thereby Andreas Schottus's Hexaemeron, diatribe 13.

text: Καὶ ἀπὸ πάντων. Deest vox illa in textu τῶν LXX, ut et in Hebr. et Vulg. aliisque, videturque Maximo ex memoria succurrisse. Habuit autem Maximus plenum Genesis locum, ut habent Sixt. Argent., etc. Quod spectat ad legem de immundis, quæ omnia bina et bina inducenda erant, ad propagandum duntaxat speciem, non etiam septena in usum sacrificiorum, vel etiam ad vescendum : nihil causæ videtur, cur illud alterum potius omissum sit a Mose, quam a senioribus additum.
anchorLine: πάντων (y) τῶν πετεινῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ τῶν καθα-
en: 'And from all.' This word is missing in the text of the Seventy, as in the Hebrew, the Vulgate and others, and seems to have come to Maximus from memory. But Maximus had the full text of Genesis, as the Sixtine and Strasbourg editions have it. As to the law about unclean animals, all of which had to be brought in two by two merely to propagate the kind, and not also seven by seven for sacrifice or even for food, there seems no reason why that other clause should have been omitted by Moses rather than added by the elders.

text: Ἀββᾶν Σωφρόνιον. Magnæ sunt dotes, ex quibus Maximus hic Sophronium commendat; ac num ipse sit, qui Cyro obstitit, promulganti novam hæresim unitionis specie, damnavitque Heraclii (sive magis Sergii) Ecthesim, cum factus esset Jerosolymorum antistes, ejusque damnandæ auctor Joanni fuit, qui post Honorium Romæ præfuit? Favet quod tantus magister ac fidei pugil, quodque locuplete instructus bibliotheca, ut et Cyro contradicere ausus sit, et sanctæ civitatis sedem adipisci potuerit, quam a Persis Heraclius nuper vindicarat. Unum exstat ejus palmare monumentum; ea nempe synodica, quam mox factus episcopus, ad Honorium urbis Romæ antistitem, et ad Sergium Constantinopolitanum scripsit : non aliam et aliam, ut male Joannes Dallæus obtrudit, in sua de Dionysii Areopagitæ scriptis, seu quæ illius nomine circumferuntur, disputatione; sed eamdem ipsam, quam Photius Honorio inscriptam habuit, Patres vero VI synodi Sergio, uti in ejusmodi encyclicis fieri consuevit. Nec aliter Sophronius, quam refert Maximus epist. ad Joannem cubicularium, sive lib. adversus Severianos, fecisse Africæ antistitem cum præfecto; retulisse scilicet ad Romanum antistitem et ad Constantinopolitanum, ut amborum nutu et consilio Severiani dogmatis moniales compescerent : uterque nimirum pro principalitate sedis Petri Romanum antistitem consulendum putavit; Constantinopolitanum vero, qua potestate pollebat in rebus ecclesiasticis ex imperii majestate et decretis sanctæ IV synodi. Magnum sane sanctumque, quod antistes Constantinopolitanus imperatorem aulamque docuisset : majus tamen atque sanctius, quod Petri ore Ecclesiam catholicam episcopus Romanus doceret.
anchorLine: καὶ διδάσκαλον κύριον ἀββᾶν Σωφρόνιον (z) τὸν ὄν-
en: 'Abba Sophronius.' Great are the gifts for which Maximus here commends Sophronius; and is he the man who withstood Cyrus when he proclaimed a new heresy under the guise of union, and condemned the Ecthesis of Heraclius (or rather Sergius), when he became bishop of Jerusalem, John being the author of its condemnation, who after Honorius presided at Rome? It favours this that so great a teacher and champion of the faith, well furnished with a library, dared to contradict Cyrus and was able to obtain the see of the holy city, which Heraclius had lately won back from the Persians. One outstanding work of his survives: the synodical letter which, soon after becoming bishop, he wrote to Honorius, bishop of the city of Rome, and to Sergius of Constantinople: not one letter and another, as John Dallaeus wrongly puts forward in his disputation on the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite or those circulated under his name, but the very same which Photius held to be addressed to Honorius, and which the Fathers of the Sixth Synod say was addressed to Sergius, as is customary in such encyclicals. Nor did Sophronius, as Maximus reports in his letter to John the chamberlain (or in the book against the Severians), act otherwise as bishop of Africa with the prefect: he referred to the bishop of Rome and to that of Constantinople, that by the will and counsel of both they might restrain the monks of the Severian doctrine. Each thought, plainly, that the bishop of Rome was to be consulted on account of the primacy of Peter's see; and the Constantinopolitan by the power he held in ecclesiastical affairs from the imperial majesty and the decrees of the holy Fourth Synod. It is great and holy that the bishop of Constantinople should have taught emperor and court; but greater and holier that the bishop of Rome should teach the catholic Church by the mouth of Peter.

text: Ἐπιστολὴ δογματική. Falsus antiquarius videatur, et qui titulum ascripsit. Potius enim scribendum συστατική, commendatitia epistola. Quanquam enim fidem explicet, id tamen omne ut rectæ jam fidei et orthodoxum Cosmam diaconum significet, dignum proinde cui Joannes cubicularius navet operam, qua gradum pristinum, quo exciderat hæresis notatus, ab episcopo suo recipiat. Ad quem dixit, adjecisse epistolam dogmaticam, quod plane de altera proxime sequente intelligendum, quæ vere tota dogmatica est; non de hac ipsa, quæ per occasionem ac velut obiter versatur in catholicæ fidei explicanda doctrina.
anchorLine: ΙΔʹ. — Τοῦ αὐτοῦ, πρὸς τὸν αὐτόν, ἐπιστολὴ δογματική (a).
en: 'Dogmatic letter.' He who ascribed the title seems a false antiquarian. For one should rather write συστατική, 'commendatory letter'. Although it sets out the faith, the whole of it signifies that Cosmas the deacon is already of sound faith and orthodox, and therefore worthy of John the chamberlain's help in recovering from his own bishop the former rank he had lost when branded with heresy. When he says he added a dogmatic letter to it, that must plainly be understood of the next letter, which is truly all dogmatic; not of this one, which deals with the exposition of the catholic faith only by occasion and in passing.

text: Θεοτίμητον πάπαν. Spectare hæc videntur ad papam Alexandrinum, in cujus diœcesi ordinatus fuerit Cosmas diaconus, et cujus auctoritate petit restitui. Fuerit is Joannes ὁ Ἐλεήμων, cujus finem episcopatus Saracenorum hæc grassatio excepit; etsi Cyro demum ejus successore Ægyptus in Arabum potestatem cessit. Τοῦ πάπα nomen, Romano duntaxat et Alexandrino episcopis, proprium mansit, ususque Phrygii, sive id ex Cyrilli legatione in concilio Ephesino, sive aliunde ortum habuerit, quod non satis liquet.
anchorLine: χρεία πρὸς τὸν θεοτίμητον πάπαν (b) ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ
en: 'The papa honoured by God.' This seems to refer to the pope of Alexandria, in whose diocese Cosmas the deacon was ordained and by whose authority he asks to be restored. He will have been John the Almsgiver, at the end of whose episcopate this Saracen raid followed, although it was only under his successor Cyrus that Egypt passed under Arab rule. The title 'papa' remained peculiar to the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, and its use at Phrygii, whether it arose from Cyril's legation at the Council of Ephesus or from elsewhere, is not clear enough.

text: Λαβεῖν καὶ γυμνάσαι. Quasi in ea collocare operam, vel exercere ac commentari, supplendo atque augendo, seu etiam declarando, quæ videbuntur lucis aliquid desiderare. Hinc forte quod Ἰωάννην Φιλόσοφον Photii antiquarius habuit, virum scilicet sæcularis militiæ, qui tamen eruditus esset in theologicis, iis præsertim quæ physicis, seu etiam metaphysicis rationibus plusculum hæreant, ut sunt illa, Περὶ τοῦ κοινοῦ καὶ ἰδίου, aliaque ad explicandam dispensationem saneque intelligendam peropportuna.
anchorLine: καὶ τοὺς θεοφυλάκτους ὑμᾶς λαβεῖν καὶ γυμνάσαι (c),
en: 'To take up and exercise.' As though to devote effort to them, or to practise and comment, supplying and amplifying or explaining what shall seem to lack some light. Hence perhaps the fact that Photius's antiquary called him John the Philosopher: a man, that is, of secular military life, who yet was learned in theology, especially in those matters that stick rather closely to physical or even metaphysical reasonings, such as the treatise On the Common and the Proper, and other works very suitable for explaining the Dispensation and for understanding it.

text: Ἔθνος ἐρημικόν τε καὶ βάρβαρον. Nempe Arabes, Mahomete duce, tumque jam Romani imperii jugulo imminentes, cum Heraclius vastando Persas (etsi illorum victor), fractis tamen ipse viribus redierat; duoque amplissima imperia pene quassata, crebrisque utrinque mutuis cladibus summe debilitata, erant. Erat gens illa recutita, quam Heraclius prænoverat eversuram Romanum imperium, etsi ille peculiarius Judæos intelligebat, eaque ratione acre illis bellum indixerat, ad idemque Dagobertum Galliæ regem atque Hispanos accenderat. Utque ex his Maximi liquet, ingens momentum Judæi attulerunt Mahometis rebus; ut nec in illis omnino cassum oraculum fuerit. Qua de re videndus V. Cl. præses Mausacius ὁ μακαρίτης. Præfatione sua ad Pugionem fidei nostri Martini Raymundi, qui ipse utiliorem operam navavit comprimendis Judæis et Arabibus, accensa eis sua fratrumque suorum opera, clarissima prædicationis face, qua ad fidem adducta complura illorum millia; cum alias ad eam cogendos non sinat pietas Christiana.
anchorLine: ρώτερον; Ἔθνος ὁρᾶν ἐρημικόν τε καὶ βάρβα-ρον (d), ὡς ἰδίαν γῆν διατρέχον τὴν ἀλλοτρίαν· καὶ
en: 'A desert and barbarous people.' That is, the Arabs under Mahomet as leader, already hanging over the neck of the Roman Empire at the time when Heraclius, after laying waste the Persians (though he was their conqueror), had come home with his own strength broken; and the two greatest empires, nearly shattered and gravely weakened by mutual defeats, stood exposed. That circumcised people was one Heraclius had foreseen would overthrow the Roman Empire (though he understood it more particularly of the Jews, and on that account declared harsh war on them, and incited Dagobert, king of the Gauls, and the Spaniards to the same). And as is clear from Maximus's words, the Jews gave great impetus to Mahomet's cause, so that in them too the oracle was not in vain. On this matter the late illustrious president Mausacius should be consulted, in the preface to the Pugio fidei of our Martin Raymundi, who himself spent useful labour in restraining Jews and Arabs, inflamed by his own and his brothers' work, a most brilliant torch of preaching, by which many thousands of them were brought to the faith, since Christian piety does not allow them to be compelled by other means.
